title: Git Flow lab
subtitle: Git Flow delivery built from blank files: Azure DevOps first (CI, central CD by source branch, approvals, versioned templates, a self-hosted agent), then GitHub Actions
intro: Companion repository lab-gitflow: one mission a day next to the platform session. The platform is trunk-based with GitOps; here you build the other model clients run — Git Flow with a push-based central pipeline. Deploys are simulated (a deployment record per environment), so nothing costs money. You write every pipeline yourself; the checks only read Azure DevOps and GitHub.
rules: Answer the recall questions before reading the mission. "I don't remember" is a valid answer.
Write every pipeline from a blank file. Official docs are fine; copying a finished pipeline is not.
Record your attempt before opening a solution. Hints or solutions opened before completion make the mission AI-assisted. Ask the instructor when you are stuck: help comes as a hint ladder.
The checks only read Azure DevOps and GitHub. Everything you create is yours to create.
No secrets in any pipeline or repository. The self-hosted agent's PAT is typed once on the agent machine and never stored in Git.

blocks.title: Project, repositories and long-lived branches
blocks.focus: Azure Repos, main and develop, default branch
blocks.objective: Put the orders service in Azure Repos with the two long-lived Git Flow branches, main and develop, and make develop the default branch.
blocks.interviewAngle: "Which branching strategy do you use and why?" — the answer starts with the long-lived branches and what each one represents.

prerequisites.notes: Project lab-gitflow already exists in the organization. The sample service is in C:\Projects\lab-gitflow\app.

reuse.note: Mirrors what the platform does with main only; here develop is added on purpose.

recall.question: Name the Git Flow branch types and what each one represents.
recall.answer: main = what runs in production (tagged per release); develop = integration of the next release; feature/* = one change, from and back to develop; release/x.y.z = stabilise a release cut from develop; hotfix/x.y.z = urgent fix cut from main. Release and hotfix end merged into main and back into develop.

recall.question: Why is develop usually the default branch in Git Flow?
recall.answer: New feature branches and pull requests should start from and target develop by default; main only receives release and hotfix merges.

steps.title: Create the app repository
steps.detail: Set the defaults once so every az devops command targets the lab project, then create the repository orders-app.
steps.command:

az repos create --name orders-app --query "{name:name, url:remoteUrl}" -o table

remoteUrl is what you add as a git remote.
steps.solution: az repos create --name orders-app returns the remoteUrl https://az400edilsonmontry@dev.azure.com/az400edilsonmontry/lab-gitflow/_git/orders-app.

steps.title: Push the service with main and develop
steps.detail: From C:\Projects\lab-gitflow, add the Azure Repos remote, push main, then create develop from main and push it. Only the first command is given.
hints: git push ado main, then git switch -c develop and git push -u ado develop.
Git Credential Manager opens a browser sign-in the first time.
steps.solution: git remote add ado <url>; git push ado main; git switch -c develop; git push -u ado develop. az repos ref list --repository orders-app --filter heads/ -o table shows both.

steps.title: Make develop the default branch
steps.detail: No command given. Change the repository's default branch to develop and prove it.

steps.solution: az repos update --repository orders-app --default-branch develop; az repos show --repository orders-app --query defaultBranch → "refs/heads/develop".

english.question: Which branching strategy did you set up for this service, and what does each long-lived branch represent?
followUps: Why is develop the default branch?
english.modelAnswer: I set up Git Flow. main always reflects production and gets a tag for every release. develop is where the next release is integrated, so it's the default branch: feature branches start from it and come back to it through pull requests. Releases and hotfixes are short-lived branches that end merged into main and back into develop, so the two never drift apart.

blocks.next: G01: the CI pipeline for every Git Flow branch.

blocks.title: CI pipeline from a blank file
blocks.focus: YAML triggers for Git Flow branches, PR trigger, artifact
blocks.objective: Write azure-pipelines/ci.yml from a blank file: it runs on develop, release/*, hotfix/* and main, installs Node, runs the tests and publishes the app as a pipeline artifact; register it as pipeline orders-ci and get a green run on develop.
blocks.interviewAngle: Clients ask you to read and fix CI YAML on day one: triggers, steps and artifacts.

prerequisites.notes: One free Microsoft-hosted parallel job (1,800 min/month): keep runs short.

reuse.note: Same skills as the R5 drill, now running for real.

recall.question: In Azure Repos, which trigger runs a pipeline on a pull request: pr: in YAML or a branch policy?
recall.answer: For Azure Repos Git the pr: keyword is ignored; PR builds come from the Build validation branch policy. trigger: covers pushes (CI).

recall.question: What is the difference between a pipeline artifact and a build artifact, and which would you publish here?
recall.answer: Pipeline artifacts (PublishPipelineArtifact / publish:) are the modern, faster storage used by pipeline resources and download:; build artifacts are the older Publish Build Artifacts task. Use a pipeline artifact.

steps.title: Write ci.yml from a blank file
steps.detail: On a feature branch of orders-app (feature/ci-pipeline), create azure-pipelines/ci.yml: trigger on develop, release/*, hotfix/* and main; ubuntu-latest; Node 20 via NodeTool@0; npm test in app/; publish app/ as the artifact named app.
steps.command:
git -C C:\Projects\lab-gitflow switch -c feature/ci-pipeline develop
code C:\Projects\lab-gitflow\azure-pipelines\ci.yml
hints: trigger: branches: include: [develop, release/*, hotfix/*, main]
steps: - task: NodeTool@0 inputs: versionSpec: '20.x' - script: npm test workingDirectory: app - publish: app artifact: app
steps.solution:
trigger:
  branches:
    include: [develop, release/*, hotfix/*, main]
pool:
  vmImage: ubuntu-latest
steps:
  - task: NodeTool@0
    inputs:
      versionSpec: '20.x'
  - script: npm test
    workingDirectory: app
    displayName: Unit tests
  - publish: app
    artifact: app

steps.title: Register the pipeline as orders-ci
steps.detail: Push the branch, then create the pipeline from the YAML without running it. Then merge to develop for now with a direct push (branch policies come in G02).
steps.command: az pipelines create --name orders-ci --repository orders-app --repository-type tfsgit --branch feature/ci-pipeline --yml-path azure-pipelines/ci.yml --skip-first-run
hints: git push -u ado feature/ci-pipeline before az pipelines create.
git switch develop; git merge feature/ci-pipeline; git push ado develop — the push triggers the run.
steps.solution: After the merge to develop the trigger starts orders-ci; az pipelines runs list --pipeline-ids <id> --branch develop -o table shows it.

steps.title: Read the run
steps.detail: Find the run on develop and open its log. Write which stage/job/steps ran and where the artifact is.
steps.command: az pipelines runs list --name orders-ci --top 3 --query "[].{id:id, branch:sourceBranch, result:result}" -o table
hints: az pipelines runs show --id <id> --open opens it in the browser.
No stages: declared means one implicit stage and one job.
steps.solution: One implicit stage, one job (Job), steps: checkout, NodeTool, Unit tests, publish. The artifact app is under the run's Related → Published.

steps.title: Break/fix (optional): a failing test
steps.detail: On a feature branch, break orderTotal (e.g. remove the rounding) and push. Predict which step fails and why the artifact is not published; then revert.
hints: Steps after a failure are skipped unless they have a condition.
A red CI is the gate that keeps develop green.
steps.solution: Unit tests fails, publish is skipped (default condition succeeded()), the run is red. Revert the change and push again.

english.question: Walk me through the CI pipeline you wrote: what triggers it, what it does and what it produces.
followUps: How do pull requests get a build in Azure Repos?
english.modelAnswer: The CI pipeline runs on every push to develop, release, hotfix and main branches. It installs Node 20, runs the unit tests and publishes the application folder as a pipeline artifact, so the same package can be deployed later without rebuilding. Pull requests in Azure Repos get their build from a build-validation branch policy, not from the YAML, which I add next.

blocks.next: G02: protect develop and main with branch policies.

blocks.title: Branch policies: PR, reviewer, build validation
blocks.objective: Require a pull request with at least one reviewer and a green orders-ci build on develop and on main, so nothing reaches them by direct push.
blocks.interviewAngle: "How do you stop a broken change from reaching main?" — branch policies with build validation is the Azure DevOps answer.

prerequisites.notes: You are the only user: allow requestors to approve their own changes, otherwise you lock yourself out.

reuse.note: The platform repository does the same with GitHub branch protection.

recall.question: Name three branch policies you would put on main.
recall.answer: Minimum number of reviewers, build validation (a required pipeline), linked work items / comment resolution / limit merge types (e.g. squash only).

recall.question: Who can bypass branch policies and why is that a risk?
recall.answer: Users with "Bypass policies when completing pull requests/pushing" permission (often project admins). It must be limited and audited, otherwise the gate is optional.

steps.title: Minimum reviewers on develop
steps.detail: Create the reviewer policy on develop (one reviewer, creator can approve because you work alone).
steps.command:
$repoId = az repos show --repository orders-app --query id -o tsv
az repos policy approver-count create --repository-id $repoId --branch develop --minimum-approver-count 1 --creator-vote-counts true --allow-downvotes false --reset-on-source-push true --blocking true --enabled true
hints: --creator-vote-counts true lets you approve your own PR.
az repos policy list --repository-id $repoId --branch develop -o table
steps.solution: The policy "Minimum number of reviewers" appears enabled and blocking on refs/heads/develop.

steps.title: Build validation with orders-ci
steps.detail: Add a build-validation policy on develop that runs orders-ci. The command group is given; complete the arguments.
steps.command: az repos policy build create --repository-id $repoId --branch develop ...
hints: --build-definition-id comes from az pipelines show --name orders-ci --query id.
--queue-on-source-update-only false --manual-queue-only false --valid-duration 720 --display-name ci --blocking true --enabled true
steps.solution: az repos policy build create --repository-id $repoId --branch develop --build-definition-id <id> --display-name ci --queue-on-source-update-only false --manual-queue-only false --valid-duration 720 --blocking true --enabled true

steps.title: The same on main
steps.detail: No command given: put the reviewer and build-validation policies on main too, then try a direct push to develop and record the error.
hints: Repeat both commands with --branch main.
git push ado develop with a new commit should be rejected (TF402455).
steps.solution: Both policies on main. A direct push fails with TF402455: Pushes to this branch are not permitted; you must use a pull request.

english.question: How do you make sure nothing reaches develop or main without review and a green build?
english.modelAnswer: Both branches have branch policies: a pull request is mandatory, it needs at least one approval, and a build-validation policy runs the CI pipeline on the merged result, so a red build blocks completion. Direct pushes are rejected. The bypass permission is limited to a couple of admins and audited.

blocks.next: G03: the first feature through develop.

blocks.title: First feature through develop
blocks.focus: feature/* → PR → build validation → squash merge
blocks.objective: Add a small feature (a minimum order value) on feature/min-order, open a PR to develop, get the policy build green, complete it with squash and delete the branch.
blocks.interviewAngle: The daily loop every team expects you to run without thinking.

reuse.note: The platform's FEAT-01 is the trunk-based version of the same loop.

recall.question: Merge commit, squash, rebase and fast-forward: which would you allow into develop and why?
recall.answer: Squash keeps develop history one commit per feature and makes reverts easy; merge commits preserve branch history; rebase/fast-forward keep it linear. Teams usually allow squash for features and a merge commit for release/hotfix back-merges.

recall.question: What should a good PR description contain?
recall.answer: What and why, how it was tested, risk/rollback notes and linked work item — enough for a reviewer who did not write it.

steps.title: Code and test the feature
steps.detail: On feature/min-order from develop: orderTotal throws a RangeError when the total is below a minOrder option (default 0). Add a test first.
hints: Add { minOrder = 0 } to the options and compare after the discount.
npm test in app/ must pass before you push.
steps.solution: A test asserting orderTotal([{price:5,quantity:1}], {minOrder:10}) throws RangeError, and the check in orderTotal after the discount.

steps.detail: Push and open the PR with auto-complete and squash.

git push -u ado feature/min-order
az repos pr create --source-branch feature/min-order --target-branch develop --title "Minimum order value" --description "Adds minOrder; tests included." --auto-complete true --squash true --delete-source-branch true

Approve your own PR: az repos pr set-vote --id <id> --vote approve
steps.solution: The PR completes once the build is green and the vote is in; the branch is deleted; develop gets one squash commit and orders-ci runs on develop.

steps.title: Explain what ran twice
steps.detail: orders-ci ran for the PR and again on develop. Write why both runs exist and what each one proves.
hints: The PR build validates the merge result before completion.
The push to develop is what feeds deployment later.
steps.solution: The policy build proves the merge result is green before it lands; the CI run on develop produces the artifact that CD will deploy.

english.question: Walk me through how a feature gets into develop in this repository.
english.modelAnswer: I branch from develop, write the change with a test, push and open a pull request to develop. The build-validation policy runs CI on the merged result, a reviewer approves, and the PR completes with a squash merge, so develop gets one clean commit per feature and the branch is deleted. The push to develop runs CI again and produces the artifact that will be deployed.

blocks.next: G04: a repository of versioned pipeline templates.

blocks.title: A versioned template repository
blocks.focus: Steps/stage template, parameters, a tag as the version
blocks.objective: Create repository pipeline-templates with templates/deploy-stage.yml (a parameterised deployment stage that simulates a deploy) and tag it v1.0.0.
blocks.interviewAngle: Platform teams ship pipeline templates like a product: versioned, reviewed and pinned by consumers.

reuse.note: Same idea as pipelines/azure-devops/templates/terraform-layer.yml in the platform.

recall.question: Which kinds of templates exist in Azure Pipelines?
recall.answer: Stage, job, step and variable templates (includes), plus extends templates (the template controls the whole pipeline — used for governance).

recall.question: Why pin a template to a tag instead of a branch?
recall.answer: A tag is immutable: consumers get the same template until they choose to upgrade; a branch changes under them and can break every pipeline at once.

steps.title: Create the repository
steps.detail: Create pipeline-templates and clone it next to the lab.
steps.command: az repos create --name pipeline-templates --query remoteUrl -o tsv
hints: git clone <url> C:\Projects\pipeline-templates
az repos list --query "[].name" -o tsv shows both repositories.
steps.solution: An empty repository you clone locally; its default branch will be main.

steps.title: Write templates/deploy-stage.yml
steps.detail: A stage template with parameters envName, environment and condition. One deployment job on the given environment, strategy runOnce: download the app artifact from the pipeline resource ci, write a deployment record (version, source branch, run name, environment) to a file and publish it as an artifact named deploy-<envName>.
hints: parameters: - name: envName type: string ...; stages: - stage: ${{ parameters.envName }} condition: ${{ parameters.condition }}
- download: ci artifact: app; the variables resources.pipeline.ci.sourceBranch and resources.pipeline.ci.runName describe what you deploy.
steps.solution:
parameters:
  - name: envName
    type: string
  - name: environment
    type: string
  - name: condition
    type: string
    default: succeeded()
stages:
  - stage: ${{ parameters.envName }}
    condition: ${{ parameters.condition }}
    jobs:
      - deployment: deploy
        environment: ${{ parameters.environment }}
        strategy:
          runOnce:
            deploy:
              steps:
                - download: ci
                  artifact: app
                - bash: |
                    mkdir -p $(Pipeline.Workspace)/record
                    echo "env=${{ parameters.envName }} build=$(resources.pipeline.ci.runName) branch=$(resources.pipeline.ci.sourceBranch)" | tee $(Pipeline.Workspace)/record/deployment.txt
                  displayName: Simulated deploy
                - publish: $(Pipeline.Workspace)/record
                  artifact: deploy-${{ parameters.envName }}

steps.title: Release v1.0.0 of the template
steps.detail: Commit on main, push, then create and push an annotated tag v1.0.0.
hints: git push origin main --follow-tags
az repos ref list --repository pipeline-templates --filter tags/ -o table
steps.solution: refs/tags/v1.0.0 appears in the ref list.

english.question: How do you share pipeline logic across teams without breaking them when you change it?
followUps: What is an extends template for?
english.modelAnswer: We keep the shared logic in a templates repository and release it with tags, like a library. Consumers reference the repository as a resource pinned to a tag, so a change only reaches them when they bump the version in a pull request. For governance we can go further with extends templates, where the template owns the pipeline structure.

blocks.next: G05: the central CD pipeline that consumes the template.

blocks.title: Central CD: pipeline resource, DEV/HML/PRD by source branch
blocks.focus: resources.pipelines trigger, repository resource at a tag, stage conditions
blocks.objective: Write azure-pipelines/cd.yml in orders-app and register it as orders-cd: triggered by orders-ci, using the template pinned to v1.0.0, with three stages whose conditions route develop → DEV, release/* and hotfix/* → HML, main → PRD. Get a deployment to DEV.
blocks.interviewAngle: "How do you decide which environment a build goes to?" — in Git Flow, by the source branch of the artifact.

prerequisites.notes: Environments DEV, HML and PRD are created automatically on the first run that targets them, or create them first in Pipelines → Environments.

reuse.note: C022 uses the same mechanics on the platform.

recall.question: What does a pipeline resource with a trigger give you that a single CI+CD pipeline does not?
recall.answer: CD runs separately from CI, starts when CI completes on chosen branches, deploys exactly the CI run's artifact and exposes its metadata (resources.pipeline.<alias>.sourceBranch, runName); one CD can serve several CIs.

recall.question: Where should the branch condition live so approvals are only requested when needed?
recall.answer: On the stage (condition: …). A stage skipped by its condition never requests the environment approval; a condition only on the job would still trigger the stage-level checks.

steps.title: Write cd.yml from a blank file
steps.detail: trigger: none; resources: pipelines (alias ci, source orders-ci, trigger on develop, release/*, hotfix/*, main) and repositories (alias templates, git lab-gitflow/pipeline-templates, ref refs/tags/v1.0.0); three stages from the template with conditions on variables['resources.pipeline.ci.sourceBranch'].
hints: - template: templates/deploy-stage.yml@templates with parameters envName, environment and condition.
condition: and(succeeded(), startsWith(variables['resources.pipeline.ci.sourceBranch'], 'refs/heads/release/'))
steps.solution:
trigger: none
resources:
  pipelines:
    - pipeline: ci
      source: orders-ci
      trigger:
        branches:
          include: [develop, release/*, hotfix/*, main]
  repositories:
    - repository: templates
      type: git
      name: lab-gitflow/pipeline-templates
      ref: refs/tags/v1.0.0
stages:
  - template: templates/deploy-stage.yml@templates
    parameters:
      envName: DEV
      environment: DEV
      condition: and(succeeded(), eq(variables['resources.pipeline.ci.sourceBranch'], 'refs/heads/develop'))
  - template: templates/deploy-stage.yml@templates
    parameters:
      envName: HML
      environment: HML
      condition: and(succeeded(), or(startsWith(variables['resources.pipeline.ci.sourceBranch'], 'refs/heads/release/'), startsWith(variables['resources.pipeline.ci.sourceBranch'], 'refs/heads/hotfix/')))
  - template: templates/deploy-stage.yml@templates
    parameters:
      envName: PRD
      environment: PRD
      condition: and(succeeded(), eq(variables['resources.pipeline.ci.sourceBranch'], 'refs/heads/main'))

sourceBranch of the CI run, not of the CD run.

english.question: How does your CD pipeline decide which environment a build goes to?
followUps: Why is CD a separate pipeline?
english.modelAnswer: CD is a separate pipeline triggered by the CI pipeline as a resource, so it deploys exactly the artifact CI produced. Each stage — DEV, staging and production — comes from a versioned template and has a condition on the source branch of that CI run: develop goes to DEV, release and hotfix branches to staging, and main to production. Stages that don't match are skipped, so they never ask for an approval.

blocks.next: G06: run deployments on your own self-hosted agent.

blocks.title: Self-hosted agent on WSL
blocks.focus: Agent pool, agent install as a service, demands, PAT hygiene
blocks.objective: Create agent pool lab-wsl, install an Azure Pipelines agent in WSL Ubuntu as a systemd service, and make the DEV stage of orders-cd run on it.
blocks.interviewAngle: Real projects run self-hosted agents for network access to private resources, tools and cost. "How do you run and secure your own agents?" is a common question.

prerequisites.notes: The agent needs a PAT with the scope Agent Pools (read, manage) for registration only. Type it in the config prompt; never save it in a file or repository, and revoke it after the agent is configured.

reuse.note: Docker and minikube already run in this WSL (see the environment notes): the agent lives next to them.

recall.question: Give three reasons to use a self-hosted agent instead of Microsoft-hosted.
recall.answer: Network access to private resources (VNet, on-prem), preinstalled tools/caches and faster builds, cost/parallelism control, compliance (data stays in your network).

recall.question: What are the main security risks of a self-hosted agent?
recall.answer: Persistent state between jobs (secrets or files left behind), any pipeline in the project can run code on the machine, the identity/credentials the machine holds, and an unpatched host. Mitigate with dedicated pools per trust level, pipeline permissions on the pool, ephemeral or cleaned workspaces and least-privilege machine identity.

steps.detail: Create the self-hosted pool lab-wsl in Organization settings → Agent pools (Add pool → Self-hosted, "grant access to all pipelines" off). Then list the pools.
steps.command: az pipelines pool list --query "[?name=='lab-wsl'].{id:id, name:name, hosted:isHosted}" -o table
hints: The pool exists at organization level; the project gets an agent queue with the same name.
Leave pipeline access off: you will authorise orders-cd explicitly.
steps.solution: lab-wsl appears with isHosted false.

steps.title: Install and register the agent in WSL

hints: ./config.sh --url https://dev.azure.com/az400edilsonmontry --auth pat --pool lab-wsl --agent wsl-01 --acceptTeeEula (paste the PAT when asked).
sudo ./svc.sh install $USER && sudo ./svc.sh start; Node must be available to the agent for the deploy steps.
steps.solution: The agent shows Online in the pool. ./svc.sh status shows active (running). Revoke the PAT afterwards: the agent keeps its own credential.

english.question: Have you run self-hosted build agents? How did you set them up and secure them?
followUps: What happens when the agent is offline?
english.modelAnswer: Yes. I created a dedicated self-hosted pool, installed the agent on a Linux machine as a service under a non-root user and registered it with a short-lived token that I revoked afterwards, because the agent keeps its own credential. The pool is not open to every pipeline: each pipeline is authorised explicitly. Only the development stage runs there; production stays on Microsoft-hosted agents. If the agent goes offline, jobs wait in the queue rather than fail, so we monitor agent status.

blocks.title: Approvals only where they are needed
blocks.focus: Environment checks, approval on PRD, stage conditions

reuse.note: The platform does the same with GitHub environment reviewers (C020).

recall.question: Name three checks you can put on an environment.
recall.answer: Approvals, branch control, business hours, invoke Azure Function/REST API, query Azure Monitor alerts, required template, exclusive lock.

recall.question: Where are approvals configured in Azure DevOps YAML pipelines?
recall.answer: On the protected resource (environment, service connection, agent pool, repository, variable group) under Approvals and checks — not in the YAML.

english.question: How do approvals work in your Azure DevOps pipelines?
followUps: Why doesn't a develop build ask for approval?
english.modelAnswer: Approvals live on the production environment, not in the YAML: anyone who deploys to it, from any pipeline, has to pass the check. I also restrict production with branch control. Each stage has a condition on the source branch, so a develop build skips the production stage entirely and never waits for an approval — the approval only appears for real production releases.

blocks.title: Cut, ship and back-merge a release
blocks.focus: release/x.y.z → HML → main → PRD with approval → tag → develop
blocks.objective: Cut release/1.0.0 from develop, deploy it to HML, merge it into main with a PR, approve the PRD deployment, tag main v1.0.0 and merge back into develop.
blocks.interviewAngle: The full Git Flow release — the story clients want to hear end to end.

recall.question: What is allowed on a release branch and what is not?
recall.answer: Only stabilisation: bug fixes, version bump, release notes. No new features — they wait in develop for the next release.

recall.question: Why must a release be merged back into develop?
recall.answer: Fixes made on the release branch would otherwise be lost in the next release; develop must contain everything that is in main.

english.question: Walk me through a release in Git Flow, from develop to production.
english.modelAnswer: I cut a release branch from develop and bump the version. The CI build of that branch is deployed to staging automatically, where we only fix bugs — no new features. When it's stable I merge it into main through a pull request; the main build goes to production after an approval on the production environment. Then I tag main with the version and merge the release back into develop, so any fix made during stabilisation is not lost.

reuse.note: FEAT-06 in the platform is the trunk-based hotfix.

recall.question: Why is a hotfix cut from main and not from develop?
recall.answer: develop contains unreleased work; branching from main ships only the fix on top of exactly what runs in production.

recall.question: A release branch is open when the hotfix is done. Where must the hotfix go?
recall.answer: Into main, and into the open release branch (instead of, or in addition to, develop), so the next release also contains it.

english.question: Production has a bug and develop already has unreleased features. How do you ship the fix?
followUps: What if a release branch is open?
english.modelAnswer: I cut a hotfix branch from main, so the fix sits on exactly what's in production, write a failing test and fix it. The hotfix build goes to staging, then I merge it into main and the production deployment waits for approval. I tag the new patch version and merge the fix back into develop — or into the open release branch — so it isn't lost in the next release.

recall.question: When is a template change a major, minor or patch version?
recall.answer: Major: breaking (renamed/removed parameter, changed behaviour consumers rely on). Minor: new optional parameter or feature with a safe default. Patch: fix without interface change.

recall.question: How would you roll a template upgrade out to twenty consumer pipelines?
recall.answer: Release the tag, upgrade one pilot pipeline, watch it, then open bump PRs for the rest (automatable); keep the previous tag available for rollback.

english.question: You own shared pipeline templates. How do you change them without breaking other teams?
english.modelAnswer: Templates are versioned with semantic tags and consumers pin a tag. I add new behaviour as optional parameters with safe defaults, release a minor version and upgrade one pilot pipeline first. The other teams bump the version through their own pull requests when they're ready, and a broken upgrade is rolled back by pointing back to the previous tag.

reuse.note: The platform's workflows are trunk-based; this one is Git Flow.

recall.question: Reusable workflow vs composite action: what is the difference?
recall.answer: A reusable workflow (on: workflow_call) is a whole workflow with jobs, called as a job (uses: owner/repo/.github/workflows/x.yml@ref), can use environments and secrets: inherit. A composite action bundles steps into one step and runs inside the caller's job.

recall.question: How do you send develop to dev and main to prd in one GitHub workflow?
recall.answer: Jobs with if: on github.ref (or on the workflow_run head_branch), each calling the deploy workflow with its environment; environment deployment branch rules make it enforceable.

steps.title: Git Flow vs trunk-based
steps.detail: Write when you would choose each, using this lab and the platform as examples.

Use the LEARNING-PATH contrast table: branching, deployment model, environment selection, rollback.
steps.solution: Git Flow: scheduled releases, regulated sign-offs, several supported versions, push deployments by branch. Trunk-based + GitOps: continuous delivery, small batches, fast feedback, Git as the source of truth with easy revert. Both: protected branches, review, build once.

english.question: When would you choose Git Flow with push deployments over trunk-based development with GitOps?
followUps: How did you build the same flow in GitHub Actions?
english.modelAnswer: Git Flow fits teams with scheduled releases, formal sign-off or several supported versions at once: develop, release and hotfix branches map naturally to environments and a central pipeline pushes each build to the right one. Trunk-based with GitOps fits continuous delivery: small changes go to main behind checks, Argo CD pulls the desired state and rollback is a revert. I've built both — Git Flow in Azure DevOps and GitHub Actions with a reusable deploy workflow and protected environments, and trunk-based GitOps on my Azure platform.
